The Toughest Animals on Earth?

A  Few animals have attracted as much popular attention in recent years as the tardigrade, a microscopic invertebrate that rarely exceeds half a millimetre in length. Viewed under a microscope, it resembles a plump, eight-legged bear lumbering through a drop of water, which explains its informal name, the 'water bear'. The German pastor Johann August Ephraim Goeze first described the creature in 1773, and four years later the Italian biologist Lazzaro Spallanzani called it il tardigrado, meaning 'slow stepper'. More than 1,300 species have since been identified, living in habitats as diverse as damp moss on city walls, Antarctic lakes and sediments on the deep ocean floor.

B  The tardigrade's reputation rests on its capacity to endure conditions that would quickly kill most other organisms. Specimens in laboratory experiments have survived temperatures close to absolute zero, brief heating to around 150°C, and pressures many times greater than those at the bottom of the deepest ocean trench. Yet it is a common misconception that tardigrades are indestructible in their everyday lives. An active, feeding tardigrade is relatively fragile; its remarkable tolerance appears mainly when it enters a dormant state known as cryptobiosis.

C  The most studied form of cryptobiosis is anhydrobiosis, or life without water. As its surroundings dry out, a tardigrade pulls in its head and legs and contracts into a compact, barrel-shaped form called a 'tun'. In this condition, its water content can fall to just a few percent of normal, and its metabolism slows to a level that is almost impossible to detect. When water returns, the animal may rehydrate and resume normal activity within hours. In one widely reported case, Japanese researchers revived tardigrades taken from a sample of Antarctic moss that had been kept frozen for more than thirty years.

D  How tardigrades protect their cells during this process has long puzzled biologists. One early explanation focused on trehalose, a sugar that helps several other drought-tolerant organisms, such as brine shrimp, to survive desiccation. However, many tardigrade species produce little or no trehalose. More recent research has identified a family of proteins found only in tardigrades, which appear to form a glass-like matrix inside cells as they dry. This process, known as vitrification, is thought to hold fragile molecules in place and prevent them from unfolding or clumping together until water becomes available again.

E  A second line of research concerns radiation. In 2016 a team led by Japanese scientists reported that one species, Ramazzottius varieornatus, possesses a protein they named Dsup, short for 'damage suppressor'. When the gene for this protein was inserted into cultured human cells, the cells suffered considerably less DNA damage from X-rays than untreated cells. The finding generated considerable excitement, since it suggested possible applications in medicine and in protecting astronauts on long missions, although such uses remain speculative.

F  The most dramatic test of tardigrade endurance took place in 2007, when dried specimens were carried into low Earth orbit aboard a European Space Agency mission and exposed directly to the vacuum of space. Many of the animals recovered after returning to Earth, and some went on to reproduce successfully. Nevertheless, survival rates fell sharply among those that were also exposed to the full intensity of ultraviolet radiation from the sun. The experiment demonstrated that tardigrades are extraordinarily resilient, but it also served as a reminder that their tolerance has limits, a point sometimes lost in enthusiastic media coverage.

Estimates suggest that at least a third of the world's mangrove area disappeared during the second half of the twentieth century, much of it converted into ponds for farming shrimp or cleared for agriculture and coastal development. Yet these efforts have had mixed results: seedlings planted on mudflats where mangroves never naturally grew often die, and researchers increasingly argue that restoring natural tidal flows is more effective than planting alone.
